newsitem.title: PUERTO RICO: Puerto Rico winners vow new push for statehood.
newsitem.headline: Puerto Rico winners vow new push for statehood.

text.p: Puerto Rico Gov. Pedro Rossello claimed an easy re-election victory on Tuesday, as did the island's non-voting representative to Washington who immediately vowed to renew a push for statehood.

Gubernatorial challenger Hector Luis Acevedo of the Popular Democratic Party conceded his loss to Rossello after just a tiny number of the island's 2 million votes had been counted. By 7:30 p.m. EST, Rossello led Acevedo 55 percent to 44 percent, with 176,000 ballots counted.
"I accept the verdict of our people," Acevedo said in a concession speech. "The people have to accept, as I do, that this has been a victory for democracy."
Thousands of supporters of Rossello and his New Progressive Party waved palm fronds and danced the macarena in the streets of San Juan to celebrate the victory.

In another race of wide interest, resident commissioner Carlos Romero Barcelo won re-election and immediately vowed to press the U.S. Congress for statehood. Early returns showed Romero the victor over challenger Celeste Benitez, with 51 to 47 percent of the vote.

Romero said he would ask Congress to give Puerto Rico permission to hold a plebescite on the controversial issue of statehood by 1998. "We're going to fight for political and economic equality," Romero said. "This is a question of dignity."
Romero is a non-voting delegate to the U.S. House of Representatives on behalf of Puerto Rico, a U.S. territory.
Rossello, who belongs to the same political party as Romero, did not comment on the statehood issue in brief remarks to the press.
In a 1993 plebiscite, 48 percent of Puerto Rican voters chose commonwealth staus, 46 percent opted for statehood and the remainder chose independence.
Elections are loud, colorful and passionate in the island of 3.6 million Spanish-speaking people. Puerto Ricans are U.S. citizens but do not vote in national elections or pay federal taxes.

Election Day is an island-wide holiday, and San Juan pulsed with a party mood as New Progressive supporters dressed in blue and the red and white-clad Popular Democrats danced in the streets surrounding their party's headquarters.

At stake in the election was the entire government of Puerto Rico -- the governorship, all the seats in its bicameral legislature, its non-voting delegate to the U.S. Congress and mayors' and municipal assembly seats in all 78 of its municipalities.
This year crime and government corruption were issues but as always they were overshadowed by Puerto Rico's perennial quandary -- its relationship with the United States.
